title: Evolution
standard_text: The evidence for evolution (fossils, anatomy, embryology, DNA); natural and artificial selection; mechanisms of evolutionary change (mutation, genetic drift, gene flow, non-random mating); adaptation and speciation. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Biology, Grade 11, University Preparation (SBI3U), Strand C: Evolution)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Biology (SBI3U) worksheets on evolution: evidence for evolution, natural selection, artificial selection, genetic drift and gene flow, adaptation and speciation. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Evolution is a change in allele frequencies in a population over generations.
key_sub: Natural selection: variation, inheritance, overproduction, differential survival.
body_html:
How to think about it

Natural selection needs four things: individuals vary, the variation is inherited, more offspring are produced than can survive, and individuals with favourable traits survive and reproduce more. Over many generations the favourable alleles become more common.

Other mechanisms also change allele frequencies: mutation (new alleles), genetic drift (chance, strongest in small populations), gene flow (migration) and non-random mating. When populations are isolated long enough to stop interbreeding, a new species forms.

Example

Bacteria in a hospital become resistant to an antibiotic. Which mechanism explains this?

Resistant bacteria survive the drug and reproduce.

Answer: natural selection

Example

A storm kills most of a small island population at random. What is the change in allele frequency called?

Chance events in small populations

Answer: genetic drift (bottleneck effect)

Common mistakes

  • Saying individuals evolve: populations evolve, individuals do not.
  • Thinking organisms change because they need to: variation comes first, then selection.
  • Mixing up homologous structures (same origin) and analogous structures (same function).

faq.a: Structures with the same basic plan because they come from a common ancestor, such as the arm of a human and the flipper of a whale.

faq.q: How is artificial selection different from natural selection?
faq.a: In artificial selection, people choose which individuals breed; in natural selection, the environment does.

items.q: In a dry area, taller cacti survive better, and the population gets taller each generation. Which type of selection is this?
items.e: One extreme is favored, so the average shifts.

items.q: Over many years, giraffes with longer necks reach more leaves and leave more offspring. Which type of selection is this?
items.e: One extreme is favored, so the average shifts.

items.q: Salmon: large males fight for mates and tiny males sneak in, but medium males do poorly. Which type of selection is this?
items.e: Both extremes are favored, so the population splits.

items.q: Galls made by flies are attacked by wasps if small and by birds if large, so medium galls survive best. Which type of selection is this?
items.e: The middle is favored, so variation shrinks.

items.q: Hunters target the largest elk antlers, and average antler size shrinks. Which type of selection is this?
items.e: One extreme is favored, so the average shifts.

items.q: Fish with medium body size survive best in a stream with both fast current and predators. Which type of selection is this?
items.e: The middle is favored, so variation shrinks.

items.q: Snails on both light sand and dark rock: light and dark shells survive, but medium shells stand out in both. Which type of selection is this?
items.e: Both extremes are favored, so the population splits.

items.q: Rock pocket mice on dark lava become darker over many generations. Which type of selection is this?
items.e: One extreme is favored, so the average shifts.
